analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from collecting or selling customers' reproductive and sexual health data except as strictly necessary.
analysis.headline: The My Body, My Data Act won 16 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats, but never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop companies from collecting, keeping, or selling personal reproductive and sexual health information — period-tracker data, pregnancy status, abortion-related searches, even location signals and algorithm-based guesses — unless it is strictly necessary to provide the service the customer asked for. It would give people the right to see, correct, and delete that data, find out exactly who it was sold to, and sue violators in court. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and arbitration clauses could not be used to block those lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose reproductive or sexual health data ends up in commercial hands: users of period and fertility apps, people who search for or buy contraception or abortion pills, and patients whose location or browsing history hints at their health choices. The bill would let them find out who holds their data, force its deletion, and sue companies that misuse it — with damages of at least $100 per violation per day, no forced arbitration, and no fees to make a request. After Roe v. Wade was overturned, this kind of data can be used to identify people who seek abortions in states where it is restricted, so the protection carries real legal weight.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of period and health apps

how_it_helps.text: Companies could collect, keep, use, or sell personal reproductive or sexual health information only when strictly necessary to provide the product or service the customer requested — covering pregnancy status, menstruation, contraception, medication abortion, surgeries, and even location data that might indicate someone tried to obtain these services.

Individuals would gain enforceable rights to access, correct, and delete their data, see a list of the specific third parties it was sold to (including data the company inferred or bought), with a 15-day deadline, no fees, and an easy online mechanism.
Companies would have to publish a clear privacy policy listing exactly which third parties they sell this data to and what those buyers do with it.

The bill could be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission and by individuals suing in court, with damages of $100 to $1,000 per violation per day or actual damages, attorney's fees, and a ban on pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers for these claims.

It would bar retaliation — companies could not deny service, change prices, or degrade quality because someone exercised these rights — and state laws giving stronger privacy protection would remain in force.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that profit from collecting and reselling this data: data brokers, ad-tech firms, and app developers whose business models rely on harvesting signals about pregnancy, contraception, and sexual activity. They would face compliance costs, lose a data set they can currently monetize, and risk statutory damages and lawsuits. Ordinary consumers would pay little or nothing directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, health app makers

drawbacks.text: The private right to sue, with statutory damages of $100 to $1,000 per violation per day, creates real litigation risk — particularly for small app developers who could face expensive suits over technical compliance, not just bad-faith data sales.

The definition of covered data is broad: it includes information a company never directly collected but inferred or extrapolated through algorithms, plus any data 'reasonably capable of being associated' with a person. Complying with that standard would be difficult and costly for companies whose analytics produce such inferences as a byproduct.

The bill exempts HIPAA-covered hospitals, doctors, and insurers, so the traditional health care system stays under the older, narrower HIPAA privacy rules; the new protection would cover apps and data brokers but leave a two-tier system with gaps on the medical side.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protection is substantial and aimed at a genuinely sensitive category of data — the kind that, after Roe was overturned, can expose people to legal jeopardy in some states. The main costs fall on the companies monetizing that data, which is the point of the bill; the compliance burden and litigation risk are real but proportionate to the sensitivity of the information. The largest honest shortcoming is the HIPAA carve-out, which leaves the formal health care system under weaker rules than the app economy. Weighing it, the bill's benefits to ordinary people clearly outweigh its costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mazie Hirono introduced the bill on May 17, 2023, joined by 12 other Democratic senators as original cosponsors, including Senator Maria Cantwell, the chair of the committee it was sent to.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; that referral is the last action recorded for the bill.
Sixteen senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill, but the committee never held a markup or vote, and the full Senate never considered it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, ad-tech companies, and app makers that collect and sell reproductive and sexual health data are better off — the data remains theirs to monetize, unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and apps selling health data

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats and no Senate Republican signed on; there was no recorded opposition or vote, since the bill never left committee.

industries.note: Their business is collecting and reselling location, browsing, and app-usage data that reveals pregnancies, contraception use, and clinic visits. The bill would bar them from collecting or selling reproductive health data at all and require deletion on request.

Advertisers currently buy targeting signals — pregnancy, ovulation, fertility-treatment searches — inferred by algorithms; the bill expressly covers inferred and algorithmic data and bans its use and disclosure.

industries.industry: Consumer health app developers (period, fertility, and sexual wellness apps)
industries.note: Apps that monetize user data would have to collect only what is strictly necessary, publish their data-sharing partners, and face statutory damages and lawsuits; some developers with genuinely minimal data practices would bear mostly compliance costs.

industries.industry: Hospitals, doctors, and health insurers (HIPAA-covered entities)
industries.note: The bill exempts them, so they keep operating under HIPAA rather than the stricter new standard — locking in the existing two-tier system in which the traditional medical sector retains broader latitude to share health data than the app economy would have.
